supplement.where: Online Supplement, Appendices B-F, PDF pp. 33-50 (printed e-1 to e-17, and the last page is printed '18'). Appendix A (pp. 30-32) belongs to the main document.
supplement.holds: Proofs of the results in Sections 4-6 (Appendices B-D), the three-point-distribution version of the model (Appendix E), and the simulation algorithms and base settings for the self-training loop (Appendix F). The paper reports no empirical statistics, so there are no standard errors anywhere.

paper_design_summary: A theory paper with no human participants and no empirical data. The authors build a Bayesian model in which a continuum of users with heterogeneous preferences choose how much information to share with an AI, trading off output fidelity against communication cost, or do the task themselves at a fixed cost. They prove that output variance falls below preference variance (homogenization), simulate a self-training loop in which retraining the AI on AI output can cause a homogenization 'death spiral' (Section 5, Appendix F), and show that AI bias can become societal bias.

studies.label: Bayesian model of human-AI interaction with numerical simulations of a self-training loop (theory)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing. No people are studied. The paper derives analytical results and varies model parameters (lambda, Gamma, the preference distribution) in proofs and simulations.
assignment.quote: To study this effect, we introduce a Bayesian framework in which heterogeneous users choose how much information to share with the AI, facing a trade-off between output fidelity and communication cost.

participants.who: No human participants. Users are a modeled continuum of preference types theta, normally distributed with mean mu_p and standard deviation sigma_p (p. 8, Section 3). The simulations discretize the preference distribution with the Lloyd-Max algorithm, base setting mu_p = 0, sigma_p = 1, M = 1001 support points, T = 100 iterations (p. e-17, Appendix F).
participants.quote: Formally, there is a continuum of users of type θ ∈ Θ, denoting a user’s specific preference about how to complete the task.
participants.locator: p. 8, Section 3 (Model Setup); simulation settings p. e-17 (PDF p. 49), Appendix F

ai_tool.name_model: Stylized AI that forms a Bayesian posterior over the user's preference and returns its posterior mean. No real model is tested. Figure 1 (p. 3) shows two abstracts of the paper generated with ChatGPT GPT-4o as an illustration only.
ai_tool.how_used: Modeled: the user sends a normal signal of her preference at a communication cost proportional to the mutual information it carries, and the AI returns the posterior mean (Eq. 2, p. 8). The user can instead do the task herself at fixed cost Gamma (Eq. 3, p. 9).

task.description: Abstract task with a one-dimensional preference over outputs. Examples given are writing an abstract (pp. 1-3, Figure 1) and a journalist writing a news article (p. 11, Example 1).

company_involvement.description: None stated. The authors list academic affiliations only (UCLA Anderson School of Management and Kellogg School of Management, Northwestern University), and the document has no acknowledgments or funding statement.

eligibility.reason: Theory paper with numerical simulations; none of the three core criteria is met. Random assignment: the paper develops a Bayesian model of users' choices, with no people assigned to AI conditions (PDF p. 1, Abstract; pp. 8-9, Section 3). People analyzed: the users are a modeled continuum, not a human sample (PDF p. 8, Section 3); M = 1001 is the number of discretized preference support points and T = 100 is the number of simulation iterations, not people analyzed (PDF p. 49, printed e-17, Appendix F). Output scoring: homogenization is the variance of the model's output distribution (PDF p. 13, Section 4.2 and Theorem 1), not a creativity or diversity score on outputs produced by participants; the two GPT-4o abstracts in Figure 1 are illustrations without such scores (PDF p. 3). Codebook Section 3 excludes theory papers from the dataset, and no context class applies.

one_line_finding: In a Bayesian model with no human data, when everyone uses AI the variance of outputs is lower than the variance of user preferences and falls as the cost of human-AI interaction rises (Theorem 1, p. 13; Figure 3, p. 14), and retraining the AI on its own output then drives output variance toward zero over 100 simulated iterations, a 'death spiral' (Section 5.1, Figure 4a, p. 16).
notes: Layout: main text pp. 1-26, references pp. 26-29, Appendix A pp. 30-32, Online Supplement Appendices B-F on PDF pp. 33-50 (printed e-1 to e-17, and the last page is printed '18'). The only empirical-looking items are Figure 1 (p. 3, two ChatGPT GPT-4o abstracts shown as an illustration and not scored) and the numerical simulations of the model (Figures 4-9, pp. 16-22, Appendix F). assignment.unit and assignment.structure are placeholders: nothing is assigned. The literature review (p. 5) cites Doshi and Hauser (2024), Wang et al. (2023), Anderson et al. (2024), and Padmakumar and He (2024) as empirical homogenization studies. These may be candidates if not already screened. candidates.json lists no arXiv id for this paper, and the document gives arXiv:2309.10448v4. The reconciler merged complementary wording from the two forms (label, summary, participants.who, ai_tool, task, reason, one_line_finding, notes) and did not count those as differences. Final review: read the complete markdown conversion, including Appendices A-F, and checked the eligibility passages, document version, page count, supplement contents, and recorded simulation settings against the PDF. No c004 challenge files were present. The design-code question is resolved by retaining 'other' for analytic theory under the current specification; it has no effect on eligibility. The reconciliation object is unchanged.
